SOURCE: "GitSwarm: Decentralized Compounding Inference", Vedant Shah, Ankur Samanta, Paras Dahal, Mikhail Plekhanov, Carole-Jean Wu, Scott Yih, Remi Munos, Rob Fergus, Jakob Foerster, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Sanjeev Arora, Jason Weston, Aaron Courville, Anirudh Goyal (Meta Superintelligence Labs, Mila, others). arXiv:2610.04862v1 [cs.AI], 4 Oct 2026. Preprint, no venue.

COVERAGE: 217,992 chars extracted. I read the main text (chars 0 to about 52,000, through the start of the references) in full. I read these appendices in full: A (related work), C (controlled tests, partly), D, E.5, F.1, G.4, G.6 with Table 13. I skimmed the headings of the remaining appendices (B, E.2 to E.4 detail, F.2, F.3, G.1 to G.3, G.5, H prompts) and did not read their body text. I did not read the reference list past the first part, and the H prompts (about 3,000 lines) only by grep. The extractor warned "Exceeded 5000 form XObject invocations... further form content is skipped", so some figure text may be missing from the extraction. Statements in the report about the unread appendices come from the main text only.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Design: homogeneous workers coordinate only through a shared, branchable Git repo; there is no central planner and no assigned roles. Each commit has a physical Git parent plus a mandatory `informed_by=` list of semantic sources, which allows cross-branch dependencies without merges.
  number: none
  setup: Section 2. Workers run asynchronously in isolated worktrees, up to C concurrent. Each episode ends in contribute, nominate or abstain. The harness handles scheduling and validation only.
  quote: "This representation allows a worker to inherit one branch while using discoveries from others, without requiring merges." Also: "Semantic dependencies are declared by workers, not independently established as causal influence."
  where: p3 (Section 2.2)
- Shared-state coordination is limited to two read-only views, neither of which assigns work. `gs_dashboard` shows the remaining budget, the workers in flight and the nomination tally. `gs_inflight` is a public activity log in which each worker announces its scope and success and abort criteria before editing. Peers can read it and cannot modify it.
  number: none
  setup: Section 2.4, Figure 2
  quote: "two interfaces that report state but do not assign work"
  where: p4
- Readout is decentralised. Workers nominate candidates, and the harness picks the commit with the most nominations (plurality, deterministic tie-break). Nomination records are kept outside the computation graph.
  number: none
  setup: Section 2.5, Eq. 2. Used for the benchmarks, not for the research tasks.
  quote: "We keep this process distributed across workers rather than delegating to privileged final judge"
  where: p4
- ProgramBench: GitSwarm beats a continued single agent at comparable compute.
  number: 79.4% vs 65.1%
  setup: 50-task stratified subset of ProgramBench (out of 200). Codex GPT-5.5-high workers, concurrency 5, budgets of 100 to 500 charged episodes. Baseline "Forced Codex" is one agent repeatedly prompted to continue.
  quote: "it achieves a 79.39% mean score, as compared to 65.12% for Forced Codex - a single Codex (GPT-5.5-High) agent repeatedly prompted to continue, at a comparable compute budget."
  where: p2
- ProgramBench scaling: score rises with the budget, but gains diminish and input-token cost grows as the repository grows.
  number: 73.1% at B=100 to 79.4% at B=500 (Codex workers); 64.6% to 71.2% from B=100 to B=300 (base GPT-5.5); Forced baseline 63.1 to 65.1%
  setup: same 50 tasks
  quote: "GitSwarm's gains diminish at larger budgets, while input-token costs grow as workers inspect an expanding repository."
  where: p6 (Fig 3)
- IMOProofBench-Advanced: GPT-5.5-high workers solve all 30 problems in one run. The authors say this does not show a unique advantage.
  number: 30/30 (28/30 at B=20; 30 at B=40 and B=80). Gemini-3.1-Pro goes from 23.3 at B=20 to 29.0 at B=160, non-monotonic with a dip at B=80. The continued bash agent solved 26.5; forced mini-SWE-agent reached at most 23.
  setup: 30 proof problems, a single run, budgets of 20 to 160
  quote: "Note that Best-of-N baselines (with oracle verifier) also reach the benchmark ceiling at lower token consumptions, so saturating this benchmark does not establish a unique advantage for GitSwarm"
  where: p6
- Reuse is measured, not just asserted. Workers cite earlier work almost always, and most ProgramBench contributions are built upon. Proof work is reused differently.
  number: 99.9% (ProgramBench) and 96.2% (proofs) of eligible episodes cite earlier work. 94.7% of ProgramBench contributions are built on, against 44.4% for proofs. The selected solution's ancestry covers 81.6 to 92.6% of the graph on ProgramBench and 21.3 to 33.0% on proofs. Git-parent ancestry alone is about one quarter of the graph.
  setup: pooled over 200 ProgramBench runs and 150 proof runs across budgets
  quote: "Git-parent ancestry accounts for only about one quarter of the graph; declared cross-branch dependencies connect most of the remainder"
  where: p9
- Artifact consumption, from execution traces rather than declarations.
  number: 79.9 to 82.5% of eligible voluntary artifact bundles reused on ProgramBench. On proofs, workers open 583 of 759 probe bundles, execute or adapt 172, and 52 of those feed the selected ancestry.
  setup: trace analysis
  quote: "They establish observed reuse, not the causal contribution of individual dependencies to performance."
  where: p9-10
- Research task RMT (Residual Matrix Transformer): two swarms beat the reference at the same training budget.
  number: held-out loss 2.890 and 2.894 vs 3.147 for the reference
  setup: 12 Codex GPT-5.6-sol xHigh workers, 72 h, 8×H200, <350M parameters, 1.3B training tokens. Forced GPT-5.6-sol reaches 2.927 using 3.0B tokens; Codex reaches 2.690 using 10.1B tokens, mostly by widening attention and scaling training.
  quote: "The two swarms achieve held-out losses of 2.890 and 2.894, compared with 3.147 for the reference."
  where: p7
- Cross-branch reuse and recovery of failed ideas in RMT. Four of six final changes came from other branches. A failed previous-token-memory idea was revisited 49.5 h later and became a temporal mixer in the final model. The best architecture's declared dependencies span 24 commits by 24 workers. A run seeded with winning commits from 3 prior runs cut the inherited dev loss from 2.909 to 2.898 in about 28 h.
  number: 49.5 h; 24 commits by 24 workers; 2.909 to 2.898
  quote: "Four of its six changes originated on other branches."
  where: p7
- Looped Transformer: a swarm improves the dev loss, and negative results get cited.
  number: dev loss 3.187 vs 3.265 reference, 3.274 direct GPT, 3.479 Codex. 395 experiments in 26 h; 74% of negative results later cited. The 128-example eval misranked 5 of 12 model pairs vs 1 at 512 examples. The winning code's dependencies span 89 commits.
  setup: 12 Codex GPT-5.5 High workers, 48 h budget, 8×H200, Huginn 308M. The runs were still in progress at writing.
  quote: "74% of negative architectural results were subsequently cited."
  where: p7-8
- NanoChat: validation BPB drops, and negative results are reused.
  number: 0.993 to 0.905 BPB with 1,465 successful evaluations; 70.1% of negative research commits cited later
  setup: 20-worker swarm, GPT-6-Astra on GB300, 16 GPUs, first 24 active hours, 5-minute training clock. The model grows to about 1.72B parameters. Baselines are single-agent Codex and Atlas-style evolutionary search.
  quote: "a 20-worker swarm reduces validation BPB from 0.993 to 0.905 through 1,465 successful evaluations."
  where: p8
- Roles emerge without assignment. Proofs shift early toward selection, while ProgramBench keeps building.
  number: the share of proof episodes devoted to selection rises from 44.2% (B=20) to 69.7% (B=160). The ProgramBench winner first appears at a median of 93.1 to 98.0% of run progress, vs 8.6 to 17.5% for proofs. About 1 in 6 ProgramBench workers abstain as redundant, vs under 2.7% for proofs.
  quote: "These patterns emerge without assigned worker roles."
  where: p10-11
- Abstention is mostly justified but does not recover the compute already spent. 97.1% of committed collisions came from a commit that landed after the worker started. Abstainers consume 6 to 7% of ProgramBench tokens.
  number: 94.9% justified (1,349 of 1,421 adjudicable traces)
  setup: ProgramBench review of 1,422 abstention traces (an LLM analyzer is used as an instrument elsewhere in the paper)
  quote: "abstention therefore prevents a duplicate commit but not the computation already spent."
  where: p48 (Appendix G.4)
- Design tradeoffs, on a small dev set (9 ProgramBench tasks, GPT-5.5-medium, B=50, concurrency 5, 3 seeds):
  number: async 62.06±2.44% in 38.0 min vs synchronous waves 63.11±0.58% in 49.3 min. Decentralised nomination 62.06% / 38.0 min, central selector 64.40±1.49% / 34.9 min, central aggregator 58.19±4.53% / 43.9 min.
  quote: "forcing a final synthesis step was thus neither more accurate nor more efficient than decentralized nomination."
  where: p11 and p53-54 (Table 13)
  Note: the central selector scored higher and ran faster than the decentralised default. The authors say the seed count is too small to claim either way.
- Synthetic tests show the operational benefit of each substrate property, with Gemini-3.1-Pro and 3 seeds. Persistence: independent baselines reach only about 70 to 75% (B=2) or 20 to 23% (k=4) relevant-record coverage, despite larger total query budgets. Branchability reduces repeated traversal. Attribution reduces the fraction of the archive that must be read to reconstruct lineages.
  quote: "despite their larger aggregate query budget"
  where: App. C.1 to C.3 (about p23-28)

LIMITS
- No causal attribution of gains to persistence, branchability or `informed_by`. The authors say a matched-run intervention would be needed. Their words: "do not isolate the resulting performance gains."
- `informed_by` is declared by the worker, so it is not proof of influence.
- The perfect proof result is a single run, and Best-of-N and Forced baselines also reach the ceiling.
- ProgramBench uses a 50-task subset. The dev-set design comparisons used three seeds and do not establish equivalence.
- RMT swarm and reference share a 1.3B-token budget, but the single-agent comparators use more tokens. The seeded run inherits earlier research. The Looped Transformer runs were unfinished. NanoChat comparisons differ in starting checkpoint and GPUs. The two-node GPT-5.6 run is not compute-matched.
- Costs: input tokens grow with repository size, redundant episodes waste compute, and GPU contention adds overhead. Matched-compute long-horizon evaluation is left open.
- The harness is still central (scheduling, validation, plurality readout), so "decentralised" applies to intellectual control only. The synthetic persistence and branch tests change the memory interface and the prompt together.
- Model names (GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-6-Astra, Gemini-3.1-Pro) are as printed in the paper.

- Global Workspace Theory: Baars 1988; Shanahan 2006 and 2008; Goyal et al., ICLR 2022 (shared global workspace).
- Inference-time scaling: Brown et al. 2024 (Large language monkeys); Snell et al. 2024; Tree of Thoughts (Yao 2023); LATS (Zhou 2024).
- Memory across attempts: Reflexion (Shinn 2023), ExpeL (Zhao 2024), Voyager (Wang 2023), MemGPT (Packer 2023), A-MEM (Xu 2025).
- Parallel-Distill-Refine (Madaan et al. 2025); Recursive Self-Aggregation (Venkatraman et al. 2025); Kim et al. 2026 (scaling test-time compute for agentic coding).
- Multi-agent systems: Du et al. 2023 (debate), MoA (Wang et al. 2025), AutoGen (Wu et al. 2023), MetaGPT (Hong et al., ICLR 2024), AgentVerse (Chen et al., ICLR 2024), Magentic-One (Fourney et al. 2024), GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al. 2024).
- Version control for agents: AgentGit (Li et al. 2025); CAID (Geng and Neubig 2026, central manager); SwarmResearch (Virk et al. 2026, Shepherd agent).
- Concurrent work: Agora (Zhang et al. 2026), a Git-backed contribution graph with multiple parents.
- Research agents: Karpathy autoresearch and nanochat; AI Scientist; AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al. 2025); AIRA2 (Hambardzumyan et al. 2026); Darwin Gödel Machine.
- Benchmarks: IMOProofBench (Luong et al. 2025); ProgramBench (Yang et al. 2026); RMT (Mak and Flanigan 2025); Huginn (Geiping et al., NeurIPS 2025).

CODE: none worth keeping. Eq. 1 (p3) defines the edge set: Git-parent edges plus extra edges for each `informed_by` source other than the parent. Eq. 2 is the plurality readout. Figure 2 shows the `gs_dashboard` and `gs_inflight` outputs.

FIGURES
- Figure 1 (p2), "Overview of GitSwarm (Schematic)": homogeneous workers inspect, extend and contribute to a shared, branchable repository. Atomic commits preserve intermediate artifacts, and semantic dependencies link work across branches. The best single figure for the note: it shows a dead-end branch being revived and three lines converging, with no orchestrator.
- Alternative: Figure 8 (p10), the winner's ancestry in the FFmpeg run, covering 83.7% of the graph.

- No embedded instructions aimed at the reader. The prompt appendix (H) contains worker task prompts such as "You MUST NOT read... its bytes", which belong to the experiment and were not acted on.
